title: LLms
content:
### What it means for the computer boy

After one year of real agentic coding (inflection point was november 2025), it seems like LLMs mostly increase velocity of code. You can do a thousand iterations very fast. Without a proper Product Manager and a clear vision, it will mostly add noise. 

I think the direction for software dev jobs is mostly to be an agent orchestrator, at least for the coming 1-2 years. Honestly no one can seriously try to predict anything after this. Humans are genuinely bad at dealing with exponentials, as we've seen with the pandemic.

So for the next 24 months, I think you need to have solid domain knowledge, good architecture knowledge, and speed-reading abilities, and you'll be able to steer the flow from the 'intelligence tap' in the direction you want it. English is the new programming language.

My observation of dealing with vast outputs of AI generated code is that the main issue is entropy. If you don't have a developer background to know what's going on, it'll drift. You'll get 5 different date/time formatters. DHH would tell you that [where we're going](https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=vDjW_dRyKXY&ra=m), we don't care about the number of date formatters, because AI doesn't care. Maybe he is right. Most of the coding good practices I know are from the era of 'attention bottleneck'; that's why you use abstractions and reusable code. But I also think AI does a better job too if the code is clean, readable, commented.

I think that with better coding harnesses, a strong typing system, agentic PR reviews, adversarial agents, test coverage, we will be able to remove most human input from the loop. We're in this very weird in-between where my day to day work is mostly: grab a ticket from JIRA, define a plan with AI in a .md file, let AI implement each step, I read and commit each of those, then I launch an agentic review of the PR while I do one full read of the PR myself. I'm monitoring, mostly. Avoiding drift.

But it is just a matter of time. I think that even if capabilities were to plateau right now (say Opus 5.5 levels of intelligence), we still have enough 'raw intelligence' to implement it in workflows and loops in order to make current software development completely unrecognizable. It just happened way too fast so we're all scrambling to find the cleanest way to implement it, but we'll all agree on the secret sauce soon enough. I came up with my current workflow by myself, it certainly is not the most efficient one, but from trial and errors I think it matches our respective abilities: AI is good at syntax and staying focused for a long time, but I still keep the wheel. As the saying goes, a computer cannot be held accountable therefore it should not make decisions. In the next 24 months I don't think see humans going fully hands off. 

I don't know what the proper AI<>coder workflow is* because no one in the industry knows yet*.** It's both an exhilarating time to be in tech, and also a period of grief, as you go to work knowing you're fighting a losing battle and that the job you trained for *already* disappeared.**

Who knows, maybe its good that finally the machines end up taking care of the computer. Maybe it was meant to be; humans built computers and struggled against them for decades, fixing bug after bug, until they finally returned them to their rightful owners. 
**Its ok buddy, a machine will take care of the computer things now. You can finally go outside and touch some grass.**


###  What it means for the wordcel boy

One thing with LLMs is that for the first time we have non-human generated text. I don't think it ever happened before, or maybe on a tiny tiny scale (I guess early text generators etc, but even that was still deterministic). So everything you read pre-2022 you know for a fact that a human took time to write it. After that, you can't know for sure. We will have one million Thélyson Orélien scandals. In a way its similar to [low background Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low-background_steel). If we want pure, unadulterated human content, we need to pick something from pre-2022. 

It affects what you read on Reddit, the Slack messages your colleague sends you, the powerpoint presentation you're being shown. It's a mess. I find it very distressing. The cost of producing *plausible* text has fallen to zero, and we don't know yet how to deal with that. 

**It's easier than ever to delegate the mental load to your colleagues by just handing AI generated output. "just read the doc I wrote" and the doc is an eleven pages wall of slop. What can you answer to this? You can't tell the guy 'you haven't even read it yourself, even less so wrote'; so you just end up copy-pasting the 11-page doc to Claude for it to give you a bullet point summary.* And maybe that's how it was meant to be; the documentation was for Claude all along, not for you.***

In a way this is what depresses me the most, way more than losing my job/part of my identity; that we're never putting the genie back in the bottle. That we will have to coexist with non-human content for the rest of our lives. 


### What to make of this

In day to day life, LLMs massively reduce friction; lets check my current subscriptions and cancel the ones I dont use; etc. 

We're ushering into a new era of very rapid technological and social change. The common theme in my career is being in tech; being doing that since my first internships. Tech is ugly now but not sure I want to do anything else; **your most realistic option is to try and ride the tiger.** I always thought that software was the cathedrals of our era. But now these cathedrals kind of build themselves.

AI is what technology was supposed to be; invisible; netflix, spotify, email, are good pieces of software as you forget about them. You don't care how the video appears on your screen; you just press play and it starts. AI pushes that one step further; you don't have to scroll the web, navigate complex UIs; you ask and its there.
